name: Ben Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy dry goods and tinned food for Kestrel Foodservice, which supplies restaurants, canteens and a couple of hospitals. I drove delivery vans for twenty years, then moved into buying seven years ago, so I'm still the junior next to Tariq, our senior buyer. My day is price lists, supplier calls and chasing late lorries. The worst bit is a Thursday when a pasta factory tells you it's short.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I like knowing a canteen cook gets what she ordered because of a call I made. I use a chatbot now and then to draft emails to suppliers, but I check everything. My wife Lena is a nurse and our kids, Jonas and Mira, are grown. The mortgage is gone, we've got savings, and I'm aiming for 65 with a bit of fishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype was always loud. Tinned tomatoes don't care about hype, and neither does the restaurant that needs forty cases by Thursday. At work I'd say let's keep the useful bits and stop the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. If the tools save me twenty minutes on emails, fine. I'd keep my job, my pay and my pension, and my cushion is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep using the chatbot for email drafts like I do now. I'd probably ask Tariq if we could try the price-comparison tool the suppliers keep pushing. Nothing dramatic, I'd put the spare time into fishing and the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pleasant, honestly. A steady job in a world that doesn't lurch. I know the quiet doesn't last in the news, but in my own life it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this version that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worry I do have is the bosses. If the company says a tool saved money, it's easy for them to freeze hiring. I'd watch that, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with any time the tools saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably spend the saved time on the phone with suppliers, which is where the good deals are. Tariq says a call beats an email every time, and I think he's right.

say: I'd say the **hype** was always loud and the useful bits are enough.
At work I'd say keep the good tools and **stop the panic**.
think: I feel **calm**, because my job, pay and pension look safe.
Mainly I'd watch whether bosses use tools as a reason to freeze hiring.
do: Keep using the chatbot for **email drafts** and check every one.
Ask Tariq to trial a **price-comparison tool**.
feel: **Pleasant** and steady, as life already is for me.
S0.quote: Tinned tomatoes don't care about hype, and neither does the restaurant that needs forty cases by Thursday.
fieldNote: Seven years from **van driver** to buyer gives him a practical view of tools.
Calm is earned by strong savings and a safe pension date.
Slight wariness of owners using tools as an excuse.

steps.text: Keep drafting supplier emails with the chatbot and check each
Ask Tariq to trial a price-comparison tool this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real this time, and it'll hit offices before warehouses. At work I'd say let's get trained on it before it gets done to us. Online I'd say rules and public support need to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy for my own corner. Comparing quotes and reordering is what software does well, and I'm junior with only seven years in buying. I can't see them cutting the senior buyer, so it's people like me who'd be squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gerda, our manager, for proper training on the ordering system instead of picking it up in corners. I'd learn what the tools can't do, like judging whether a small supplier will really deliver. I'd also make sure our union steward knows what's happening to buyers' targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow squeeze rather than a shock. That's easier to live with. I'd say uneasy, with the savings keeping it from being worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Priya, the young trainee in purchasing. She'll be asked to do twice the work with a tool and no pay rise. I'd tell her to learn it, and to keep a note of what she delivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let software choose suppliers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure I'd trust the machine to pick a supplier. I'll use a machine to draft my emails, but I won't let one decide which supplier we trust with a restaurant's Saturday night.

say: I'd say it's **real**, and offices feel it before warehouses.
I'd tell colleagues to get **trained** before it's done to us.
think: Comparing quotes is what software does well, so I'm **uneasy** as the junior.
I think the junior buyers would be **squeezed**, not the senior one.
do: Ask Gerda for **proper training** on the ordering system.
Learn what tools can't do, like judging a **small supplier**.
Tell our steward about changes to **buyers' targets**.
feel: A **slow squeeze**, easier to live with than a shock.
S1.quote: I'll use a machine to draft my emails, but I won't let one decide which supplier we trust with a restaurant's Saturday night.
fieldNote: Sees himself as **squeezed junior**, with Tariq protected by seniority.
Draws a clear line on what stays human: supplier trust.

steps.text: Ask manager Gerda for proper training on the ordering system
Tell the union steward what is changing in buyers' targets
Keep calling small suppliers to judge if they will deliver

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not long for governments or families to change course. At work I'd say let's ask Gerda now what the plan is. Online I'd say pay and protection have to be talked about this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. Everything on my desk is thinking work, and it would be done better and cheaper. I'm 58 and junior, so I can't count on being kept, and the robots come three years later, which doesn't help a desk man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending, put the extra into the pension pot and clear the last of the car loan. I'd ask Gerda if there's an early-leaving deal at 60. And I'd talk to the union about a payout before layoffs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy. Two years is not enough time for a country to change its mind, let alone for me to start a new career at 60. But we're not skint and Lena's wage is secure, which keeps the fear from running wild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would say stay calm and keep working until the offer comes. She sees a lot of people in bad moments, and she says panic makes it worse. I'd have to listen to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd cut first is the holiday abroad and the second car insurance. Our savings are good but I'd rather keep them for later.

say: I'd say two years is **too short** for governments or families to adjust.
I'd ask Gerda what **the plan** is.
think: All my desk work could be done better and cheaper, so I'm **anxious**.
Being 58 and junior, I can't count on being **kept**.
do: Cut spending and clear the **last car loan**.
Ask Gerda about an **early-leaving deal** at 60.
Talk to the union about a **payout** before layoffs.
feel: Heavy, but Lena's secure wage keeps the **fear** from running wild.
S2.quote: Two years is not enough time for a country to change its mind, let alone for me to start a new career at 60.
fieldNote: His **cushion** and Lena's nurse wage hold anxiety below alarm.
Listens to his wife's calm over his own worry.
Early-leaving deal is the key lever.

steps.text: Skip the holiday abroad and drop the second car insurance
Clear the last car loan within six months
Ask Gerda about an early-leaving deal at 60
Talk to the union about a payout before layoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build a real plan, and short enough that I won't waste it arguing about whether it's coming. At work I'd say let's get ahead of it. Online I'd back training schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be 63 by 2031, close enough to leave on my terms. So I'm anxious but not frightened. I'd still want a safety net, because the pension isn't huge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more, get properly good at them, and ask to move into supplier relations, which is more human. I'd save harder for three years, then ask about leaving at 62. And I'd help Mira, who teaches, think about her own plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels workable. Five years is a stretch of time I can actually use. I'd be annoyed, but busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas, who's an electrician, he's got a few extra years in his favour, but not to be smug. His job's safer than mine, not safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would change my mind is if the company starts hiring fewer buyers in year two. Then I'd stop waiting and ask for the leaving deal.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **real plan**.
At work I'd say let's **get ahead** of it, not wait for orders.
think: By 2031 I'd be **63**, close enough to leave on my terms.
My pension isn't huge, so I'd want a **safety net**.
do: Get properly good at **AI tools** and ask for supplier-relations work.
Save hard for three years, then ask about leaving at **62**.
Help Mira, who teaches, think about **her plan**.
feel: **Workable**, with time I can actually use.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build a real plan, and short enough that I won't waste it arguing about whether it's coming.
fieldNote: Time converts his fear into **planning**, which is the main thing that changes between scenarios.
Watches the company's hiring as the **trigger** to act, which gives him a clear rule.
Cares about his grown kids' futures.

steps.text: Practise AI tools weekly until they are second nature
Ask to move into supplier relations work
Bank every extra payslip for three years
Ask about leaving at 62 if hiring slows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it. At work I'd say nobody should sit still. Online I'd say governments should start retraining and income support now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy for my kids rather than me. Ten years means I'll have retired before it bites, but my son and daughter will be right in the middle of it. That's what I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at 65 as planned, maybe a year later if the pension looks thin. I'd help Jonas and Mira think about work that's hands-on or hard to automate. And I'd keep using AI at work in a small way so I'm not a fossil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels mostly fine for me, though heavy for the young. I'd be the old guy with advice nobody asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Mira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mira not to stake everything on teaching a subject a machine can do, and to keep other options. She'd roll her eyes. She might also listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your retirement look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement would be fishing, a bit of volunteering at the food bank, which I know from the other side. I'd like to still be useful.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if people use it.
I'd call for retraining and **income support** now.
think: Ten years means I'm retired before it bites, so I'm **uneasy** for my kids.
I'd be the old guy giving **advice** nobody asked for.
do: Retire at **65**, or a year later if the pension looks thin.
Steer Jonas and Mira towards **hard-to-automate** work.
Keep using **AI** in small ways at work.
feel: Mostly **fine** for myself, heavier for the young.
S4.quote: Ten years means I'll have retired before it bites, but my son and daughter will be right in the middle of it.
fieldNote: Willing to work a year longer if the pension needs it.
Imagines food-bank volunteering, tied to his work in food.

steps.text: Retire at 65 as planned, or a year later

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because it's too fast for anyone to arrange a fair deal. What would help is a payout scheme for older workers, proper retraining that isn't a joke, and unions with a seat at the table. A government that says plainly what it will do would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't all against it. I use the tools, I just want them used fairly. I'm not scared of the machine, I'm scared of the owners who'll hide behind it when they cut the wage bill. I'd like the people who own the companies to be asked the same questions as the workers.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the machine, I'm scared of the owners who'll hide behind it when they cut the wage bill.
portrait: **Ben Ziegler**, 58, a junior buyer of dry goods for Kestrel Foodservice after twenty years driving delivery vans.
He is **left-leaning**, wants unions and public support, and uses a chatbot now and then.
His mortgage is gone, savings are strong and his wife Lena is a **nurse**, so fear is cushioned.
Moods run from **calm** in the plateau case to anxious in the 2-year and 5-year cases.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because it is too fast for a fair deal for older workers.
whatWouldHelp: A **payout scheme** for older workers and retraining that actually works.
Unions with a **seat at the table**, and a government that says plainly what it will do.
